docs.title: FF4K - Feature Flags for Kotlin
docs.text: FF4K is a Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) implementation of the popular FF4J (Feature Flipping for Java) library. It brings robust feature flagging capabilities to the Kotlin ecosystem, supporting multiplatform projects.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Kotlin Multiplatform: Designed to work across different platforms supported by Kotlin (JVM, Android, Native, etc.).
  • Type-safe Properties: Strongly typed property definitions (String, Int, Boolean, etc.).
  • Flipping Strategies: Gradual rollouts, A/B testing, and user targeting with built-in strategies.
  • Serialization Support: Built-in support for kotlinx.serialization.
  • Extensible: Easily implement custom storage backends (Redis, SQL, etc.) and custom strategies.
  • DSL: Intuitive Domain Specific Language for configuration.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add the dependency to your build.gradle.kts:

dependencies {
    implementation("com.yonatankarp:ff4k-core:<version>")
}

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
suspend fun main() {
    val ff4k = ff4k {
        features {
            feature("dark-mode") {
                isEnabled = true
                description = "Enable dark mode theme"
            }
        }
    }

    // Check feature status
    ff4k.ifEnabled("dark-mode") {
        // ...
    }
}

Check out the Usage guide for more details.

docs.title: Extending FF4K
docs.text: FF4K is designed to be extensible. You can implement custom storage backends for features and properties to persist your flags in databases, remote services (like Redis, Consul), or local files.

docs.title: Implementing a Feature Store
docs.text: To create a custom feature store, implement the FeatureStore interface. For convenience, it is highly recommended to extend AbstractFeatureStore, which handles most of the common logic and boilerplate.

docs.title: Using AbstractFeatureStore
docs.text:
AbstractFeatureStore provides default implementations for group management, permission handling helper methods, and validation. You primarily need to implement the core CRUD operations.

class MyCustomFeatureStore : AbstractFeatureStore() {

    // Helper map to simulate a DB for this example
    private val db = mutableMapOf<String, Feature>()

    override suspend fun get(featureId: String): Feature? {
        return db[featureId]
    }

    override suspend fun getAll(): Map<String, Feature> {
        return db.toMap()
    }

    // Using the 'plusAssign' operator for creation (store += feature)
    override suspend fun plusAssign(feature: Feature) {
        if (feature.uid in db) {
            throw FeatureAlreadyExistsException(feature.uid)
        }
        db[feature.uid] = feature
    }

    // Using the 'minusAssign' operator for deletion (store -= featureId)
    override suspend fun minusAssign(featureId: String) {
         if (featureId !in db) {
            throw FeatureNotFoundException(featureId)
        }
        db.remove(featureId)
    }

    override suspend fun update(feature: Feature) {
         if (feature.uid !in db) {
            throw FeatureNotFoundException(feature.uid)
        }
        db[feature.uid] = feature
    }

    override suspend fun clear() {
        db.clear()
    }

    // ... implement other abstract methods ...
}

docs.title: Implementing a Property Store
docs.text:
Similarly, to create a custom property store, implement the PropertyStore interface.

class MyCustomPropertyStore : PropertyStore {
   // Implement interface...
}

docs.title: Verifying Your Implementation
docs.text: It is critical to ensure your custom store behaves correctly. FF4K provides a Contract Test Suite that you can use to automatically verify your implementation against the expected behavior.

docs.title: Registering Your Store
docs.text:
Once implemented, pass your custom store to the ff4k configuration function.

suspend fun main() {
    val ff4k = ff4k(
        featureStore = MyCustomFeatureStore(),
        propertyStore = MyCustomPropertyStore()
    ) {
        // ...
    }
}

docs.title: Implementing a Flipping Strategy
docs.text:
To create a custom flipping strategy, implement the FlippingStrategy interface. For an overview of built-in strategies, see Flipping Strategies.

@Serializable
@SerialName("timeBasedStrategy")
data class TimeBasedStrategy(
    val startHour: Int,
    val endHour: Int
) : FlippingStrategy {
    override suspend fun evaluate(
        featureId: String,
        store: FeatureStore?,
        context: FlippingExecutionContext
    ): Boolean {
        val currentHour = Clock.System.now()
            .toLocalDateTime(TimeZone.currentSystemDefault())
            .hour
        return currentHour in startHour until endHour
    }
}

docs.title: Registering for Serialization
docs.text:
If you need JSON serialization support for your custom strategy, register it in a custom serializers module and combine it with the built-in module. See Serialization for more details on ff4kSerializersModule.

val customSerializersModule = SerializersModule {
    polymorphic(FlippingStrategy::class) {
        subclass(TimeBasedStrategy::class, TimeBasedStrategy.serializer())
    }
}

val json = Json {
    serializersModule = ff4kSerializersModule + customSerializersModule
}

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: Properties in FF4K allow you to manage configuration values alongside your feature flags. Unlike feature flags which are boolean, properties can hold values of various types.

docs.title: Built-in Property Types
docs.text:
FF4K comes with support for common data types out of the box:

  • PropertyString
  • PropertyInt
  • PropertyLong
  • PropertyDouble
  • PropertyFloat
  • PropertyBoolean
  • PropertyByte
  • PropertyShort
  • PropertyBigInteger
  • PropertyBigDecimal
  • PropertyLocalDate
  • PropertyLocalDateTime
  • PropertyInstant
  • PropertyLogLevel

docs.title: Defining Properties in DSL
docs.text:
You can define properties within the properties block of the ff4k DSL.

suspend fun main() {
    val ff4k = ff4k {
        properties {
            property("app-title") {
                value = "My Awesome App"
            }

            property("max-connections") {
                value = 10
                description = "Maximum number of concurrent connections"
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Retrieving Properties
docs.text:
To retrieve a property, use the property method. You should specify the expected type.

// Get the property object
val titleProp: Property<String>? = ff4k.property<String>("app-title")
println("Title: ${titleProp?.value}")

// Get value directly (safe)
val maxConns: Int? = ff4k.property<Int>("max-connections")?.value

docs.title: Creating Custom Properties
docs.text: If the built-in types don't meet your needs, you can create custom property types by implementing the Property<T> interface or extending AbstractProperty<T>.

docs.title: 1. Implement the Interface
docs.text:
You need to implement Property<T>. It's recommended to make your implementation a data class and include serialization support.

@Serializable
data class PropertyColor(
    override val name: String,
    override val value: String, // Storing hex code as string
    override val description: String? = null,
    override val fixedValues: Set<String> = emptySet(),
    override val readOnly: Boolean = false
) : Property<String>

docs.title: 2. Using Custom Properties
docs.text:
You can manually add custom properties to the store. Here is a complete example of how to register and use a custom property type:

suspend fun main() {
    // 1. Initialize your property store
    val myPropertyStore = InMemoryPropertyStore()

    // 2. Initialize FF4K with your store
    val ff4k = ff4k(propertyStore = myPropertyStore) {
        // ... other configuration ...
    }

    // 3. Create your custom property
    val brandColor = PropertyColor(
        name = "brand-color",
        value = "#FF5722",
        description = "Primary brand color"
    )

    // 4. Add it to the store manually
    myPropertyStore += brandColor

    // 5. Retrieve and use it
    val storedColor = ff4k.property<String>("brand-color")
    println("Brand Color: ${storedColor?.value}") // Output: #FF5722
}

docs.title: Flipping Strategies
docs.text: Flipping strategies allow you to control when a feature is enabled based on dynamic conditions, rather than just a simple on/off toggle.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A FlippingStrategy is evaluated each time a feature is checked. This enables use cases like: - Gradual rollouts (percentage-based) - User-specific targeting - A/B testing - Time-based feature availability

docs.title: AlwaysTrueFlippingStrategy
docs.text: Always returns true. Useful as a base case in composite strategies.

docs.title: AlwaysFalseFlippingStrategy
docs.text: Always returns false. Useful as a base case in composite strategies.

docs.title: PonderationStrategy
docs.text:
Enables a feature based on a random percentage. Each evaluation is independent - the same user may get different results on subsequent calls.

feature("gradual-rollout") {
    ponderationStrategy(0.25) // 25% chance of being enabled
}

// Or using integer percentage
feature("gradual-rollout") {
    ponderationStrategy(25) // 25% chance
}

docs.title: UserPonderationStrategy
docs.text:
Enables a feature for a consistent percentage of users. The same user always gets the same result (sticky sessions), making it ideal for A/B testing and gradual rollouts.

Requires ContextKeys.USER_ID in the execution context.

feature("beta-feature") {
    userPonderationStrategy(0.10) // 10% of users
}

// Or using integer percentage
feature("beta-feature") {
    userPonderationStrategy(10) // 10% of users
}

// Checking with user context
val context = FlippingExecutionContext(ContextKeys.USER_ID to currentUserId)
ff4k.check("beta-feature", context)

docs.title: AllowListStrategy
docs.text:
Enables a feature only for specific users. All other users will have the feature disabled.

Requires ContextKeys.USER_ID in the execution context.

feature("vip-feature") {
    allowListStrategy {
        +"user-123"
        +"user-456"
        add("user-789")
    }
}

docs.title: DenyListStrategy
docs.text:
Disables a feature for specific users. All other users will have the feature enabled.

Requires ContextKeys.USER_ID in the execution context.

feature("new-ui") {
    denyListStrategy {
        +"problematic-user-1"
        +"problematic-user-2"
    }
}

docs.title: Composite Strategies
docs.text: Combine multiple strategies using logical operators.

docs.title: AndStrategy
docs.text:
All strategies must evaluate to true.

val strategy = strategyA and strategyB // Both must be true

docs.title: OrStrategy
docs.text:
At least one strategy must evaluate to true.

val strategy = strategyA or strategyB // Either can be true

docs.title: NotStrategy
docs.text:
Inverts the result of a strategy.

val strategy = !strategyA // Inverts the result

docs.title: Combining Strategies
docs.text:
You can chain multiple operators to create complex conditions:

feature("complex-feature") {
    flippingStrategy = (strategyA and strategyB) or !strategyC
}

For creating custom strategies, see Extending FF4K.

docs.title: Contract Testing
docs.text: The ff4k-contract-test module provides a suite of reusable tests to verify that your custom FeatureStore and PropertyStore implementations adhere to the FF4K specification. This ensures consistency and reliability across different storage backends.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
First, add the contract test dependency to your project.

Gradle (Kotlin DSL)

dependencies {
    testImplementation("com.yonatankarp:ff4k-contract-test:<version>")
}

docs.title: Testing a Feature Store
docs.text:
To test your custom FeatureStore, create a test class that extends FeatureStoreContractTest and implement the createStore method.

class MyCustomFeatureStoreTest : FeatureStoreContractTest() {

    // This method is called before each test to provide a fresh store instance
    override suspend fun createStore(): FeatureStore {
        // Return a fresh instance of your store
        // If your store relies on an external DB, ensure it's cleaned up here
        return MyCustomFeatureStore()
    }
}

The FeatureStoreContractTest will automatically run a comprehensive set of tests covering: - basic CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) - toggling features - group operations (enable/disable group, add/remove from group) - permissions - error handling (e.g., throwing correct exceptions for missing features) - concurrency handling

docs.title: Testing Properties
docs.text:
To test custom Property implementations, you can extend PropertyContractTest.

class MyPropertyTest : PropertyContractTest<String, MyStringProperty>() {
    override val serializer = MyStringProperty.serializer()

    override fun create(
        name: String,
        value: String,
        description: String?,
        fixedValues: Set<String>,
        readOnly: Boolean
    ) = MyStringProperty(name, value, description, fixedValues, readOnly)

    override fun sampleName() = "test-prop"
    override fun sampleValue() = "value"
    override fun otherValueNotInFixedValues() = "other-value"
    override fun fixedValuesIncludingSample(sample: String) = setOf(sample, "other")
}

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
Run your tests as you normally would use Gradle:

./gradlew test

docs.title: Usage Guide
docs.text: This guide covers the core concepts and usage patterns of FF4K.

docs.title: Initialization
docs.text:
The entry point for FF4K is the ff4k DSL function. It allows you to configure features and properties and returns an FF4k instance.

suspend fun main() {
    val ff4k = ff4k {
        // Configuration block
    }
}

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
The ff4k function accepts several optional arguments to customize behavior:

suspend fun main() {
    val ff4k = ff4k(
        autoCreate = true,                // Automatically create missing features (default: false)
        featureStore = InMemoryFeatureStore(), // Custom feature store (default: InMemory)
        propertyStore = InMemoryPropertyStore() // Custom property store (default: InMemory)
    ) {
        // ...
    }
}
  • autoCreate: If set to true, querying a feature that doesn't exist will automatically create it in the store (disabled by default).
  • featureStore: The backend storage for feature flags.
  • propertyStore: The backend storage for properties.

docs.title: Defining Features
docs.text:
Features are boolean flags that can be toggled on or off. You can define them within the features block.

suspend fun main() {
    val ff4k = ff4k {
        features {
            // Minimal definition
            feature("simple-feature")

            // Detailed definition
            feature("advanced-feature") {
                isEnabled = true
                description = "Controls the new dashboard layout"
                group = "ui-beta"
                permissions("ADMIN", "BETA_TESTER")
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Feature Attributes
docs.text:
• uid: Unique identifier for the feature.
  • isEnabled: Initial state of the feature (default: false).
  • description: Human-readable description.
  • group: Group name for organizing features.
  • permissions: List of roles/permissions required to access the feature.

docs.title: Defining Properties
docs.text:
Properties are key-value pairs that can store configuration data. They are strongly typed.

suspend fun main() {
    val ff4k = ff4k {
        properties {
            // String property
            property("api-url") {
                value = "https://api.example.com"
            }

            // Integer property with constraints
            property("max-retries") {
                value = 3
                description = "Max API retries"
                fixedValues(1, 3, 5) // Value must be one of these
                readOnly = true // Prevent runtime modification
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Checking Features
docs.text: There are several ways to check the status of a feature.

docs.title: Boolean Check
docs.text:
The check method returns a boolean indicating if the feature is enabled.

if (ff4k.check("dark-mode")) {
    enableDarkMode()
}

docs.title: Functional Style
docs.text:
The ifEnabled and ifEnabledOrElse extension functions provide a more functional approach.

// Execute only if enabled
ff4k.ifEnabled("dark-mode") {
    enableDarkMode()
}

// Execute one or the other
ff4k.ifEnabledOrElse("dark-mode",
    enabled = { 
        println("Dark mode is ON") 
    },
    disabled = { 
        println("Dark mode is OFF") 
    }
)

docs.title: Managing Groups
docs.text:
You can perform operations on entire groups of features.

// Enable all features in the 'ui-beta' group
ff4k.enableGroup("ui-beta")

// Disable all features in the 'ui-beta' group
ff4k.disableGroup("ui-beta")

docs.title: Runtime Modification
docs.text:
If your store supports it (like the default InMemoryFeatureStore), you can modify features at runtime.

// Enable a feature
ff4k.enable("my-feature")

// Disable a feature
ff4k.disable("my-feature")

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text: FF4K provides pre-configured serialization support for all built-in types using kotlinx.serialization.

docs.title: FF4kJson
docs.text:
FF4kJson is a pre-configured Json instance ready to use for serializing and deserializing FF4K types (features, properties, strategies).

// Serialize a feature
val json = FF4kJson.encodeToString(feature)

// Deserialize a feature
val feature = FF4kJson.decodeFromString<Feature>(json)

Configuration: - Includes ff4kSerializersModule for polymorphic serialization of all FF4K types - ignoreUnknownKeys = true for forward compatibility - prettyPrint = true for readable output

docs.title: ff4kSerializersModule
docs.text:
If you need to customize the Json configuration or combine with your own serializers, use ff4kSerializersModule directly:

val customJson = Json {
    serializersModule = ff4kSerializersModule + myCustomSerializersModule
    prettyPrint = false // Override defaults as needed
    encodeDefaults = true
}

The module includes serializers for: - All Property subtypes (PropertyInt, PropertyString, PropertyBoolean, etc.) - All FlippingStrategy subtypes (AndStrategy, OrStrategy, PonderationStrategy, etc.)

For registering custom types, see Extending FF4K.
